headline: A strong, windy storm arrives Wednesday evening into Thanksgiving morning with gusts to 50–55 mph on the coast and North Interior, Wind Advisories along the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Puget Sound, heavy mountain rain and snow, and continued coastal flooding from some of the year's highest tides.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: A front moving ashore Wednesday morning brings on-and-off showers, then rain and wind pick up along the coast by early evening as the next system's warm front lifts north. Rain spreads across the interior overnight, though Sequim sits in the Olympic rain shadow and should see less than the roughly 1 inch expected in other lowlands. A Wind Advisory runs 4 PM Wednesday to 11 AM Thursday for the eastern and western Strait of Juan de Fuca, the Lake Crescent/US 101 area, Port Townsend, the San Juans, Whidbey and the north Sound lowlands, with the strongest gusts of 50 to 55 mph on the coast and North Interior; Seattle, Kitsap, Tacoma and Olympia are under a Wind Advisory from 8 PM Wednesday to noon Thursday, with south-southeast winds of about 17 to 23 mph and gusts near 40 mph overnight. A Winter Storm Warning covers the Whatcom and Skagit County Cascades from 7 PM Wednesday to 4 AM Friday.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Wind and rain continue Thanksgiving morning, then the trailing cold front sweeps through Thursday afternoon, bringing showers, perhaps an isolated thunderstorm, and gradually easing winds (Seattle gusts dropping to around 30 mph). Storm totals reach up to 2 inches on the coast, 2 to 4 inches in the Olympics, 2 to 3 inches in the Cascades and around an inch in the lowlands outside the rain shadow. Widespread river flooding is not expected, but the Skokomish River in Mason County is forecast to reach moderate flood stage, with a River Flood Warning from Wednesday afternoon through Friday evening. Another, weaker system arrives later Friday.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Computer forecasts show a brief break with weak high pressure over the weekend, but it will be hard to go more than about 12 hours without some chance of rain. By early next week, a broad dip in the jet stream settles offshore and sends another parade of storms onshore, keeping things unsettled into Tuesday.

coast: Coastal flooding remains the headline hazard through the end of the week as some of the year's highest tides combine with storm surge and high surf. A Coastal Flood Warning runs until 4 PM Wednesday for the eastern and western Strait of Juan de Fuca (including Sequim and Port Angeles) and the Washington coast, followed by a Coastal Flood Watch from late Wednesday night through Thursday afternoon for the Strait, Port Townsend and the coast; a Coastal Flood Warning runs 3 AM to 10 AM Thursday for Seattle, Everett, Shoreline/Lynnwood, Kitsap, Island County, northern Hood Canal, the San Juans and the Pierce, King, Skagit and Whatcom lowlands, and the San Juans also have a warning until 10 AM and an advisory until 4 PM Wednesday. A High Surf Advisory covers the coast until 4 PM Wednesday. On the water, a Storm Warning covers all coastal waters and Gale Warnings cover the east and west entrances of the Strait, Admiralty Inlet and the northern inland waters until 4 AM Thursday, with Small Craft Advisories for the central Strait, Puget Sound, Hood Canal and the Grays Harbor bar; an isolated thunderstorm is possible over the coastal waters Thursday afternoon. Coastal seas of 15 to 20 feet ease to 10 to 15 feet late Thursday into Friday and below 10 feet over the weekend, with a brief lull Friday before weekend systems may stir winds and seas up again.
watch_for: Thursday morning's high tide (3–10 AM), when storm surge and wind add to coastal flooding along the Strait and Puget Sound
Gusts of 40–55 mph Wednesday night into Thursday morning, strongest on the coast and North Interior
Skokomish River flooding in Mason County through Friday evening
confidence: Confidence is high through Thursday, with no major changes from earlier forecasts and rain totals in the same range, while the weekend break and the timing of next week's storms are less certain.
